strengths: ER-KD is a simple, inexpensive extension that uses teacher prediction entropy to weight individual distillation losses. It requires no additional learned module or inference computation, and its integration with both logit and feature distillation is clearly formulated.

The reported improvements are promising across diverse settings. For example, Tiny-ImageNet accuracy increases from 56.00% to 59.93%, and COCO AP with a MobileNetV2 student increases from 30.13 to 31.67. Improvements also occur when augmenting stronger methods such as MLD and FCFD.

The evaluation covers seven CIFAR-100 teacher–student pairs, several distillation frameworks, transformer-to-CNN transfer, and object detection. Tables 1–2 report five-run averages, while Table 4 reports three-run averages, providing more evidence than isolated single-run comparisons.

The manuscript is generally easy to follow, acknowledges relevant sample-reweighting methods, attributes its datasets and underlying distillation frameworks, and provides a public code link. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b05/review-experiment-rnbk9d3k/call-b415ce047f8c47a58c32ff831f005a01/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central experimental confound is unresolved: Eq. (4) uses unnormalized entropy, changing both sample weighting and the overall strength of distillation. Eq. (6) additionally changes the balance between instance, batch, and class losses. Without a constant weight matched to mean entropy, normalized entropy weights, and a comparably tuned baseline loss coefficient, the improvements cannot be attributed specifically to prioritizing high-entropy samples. This is consequential because sample prioritization is the principal contribution.

The methodological advance over established sample reweighting is modest, and the experiments do not establish why entropy is the appropriate choice. Although Section 2 discusses focal loss, hard-example mining, and RW-KD, the ablation only varies the entropy temperature between 3 and 5. Comparisons with simple confidence-, margin-, or loss-based weights would better establish the contribution beyond a particular weighting heuristic.

The proposed explanation is stronger than its supporting evidence. Lower entropy in temperature-softened student predictions does not establish miscalibration or show that overconfidence causes the accuracy gap. Figures 2–3 provide useful correlations, but no calibration measurements or controlled intervention substantiate this causal account. Likewise, high teacher uncertainty need not imply useful dark knowledge. The loss-landscape comparisons lack sufficient information about perturbation directions and normalization to support the claimed robustness and generalization conclusions.

The results support improvement in many settings, but stronger claims need qualification. Several gains over advanced methods are only 0.05–0.3 percentage points, and Table 1 includes regressions, yet no standard deviations or confidence intervals accompany the averages. Table 4 compares only against vanilla KD, so it supports transfer to detection but does not establish the conclusion's claim of state-of-the-art detection performance.

Important implementation details remain unclear: the complete supervised-plus-distillation objective and its coefficients, transformer teacher pretraining and fine-tuning, and how entropy weighting is applied to detection proposals and losses. Algorithm 1 also passes probabilities rather than log probabilities to PyTorch's F.kl_div and omits the unreduced output needed for sample weighting. These pseudocode errors are locally correctable, but the missing training details materially hinder reproduction and assessment of comparison fairness.
